questions.stem: In India, rice, maize and jute are primarily grown during which cropping season?
questions.explanation: Kharif (monsoon) crops are sown with the onset of the SW monsoon in June and harvested in October-November. Examples: rice, maize, jowar, bajra, ragi, cotton, jute, groundnut. Rabi (winter) crops are sown in October-November and harvested in March-April — wheat, barley, gram, mustard, peas. Zaid is the short summer season (March-June) for cucumber, musk-melon, moong, fodder.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: India's largest producer of wheat — the grain belt of the country — is:
questions.explanation: Uttar Pradesh is India's largest wheat producer by volume (~30 % of national output). In terms of yield per hectare, Punjab and Haryana lead — thanks to irrigation, short-duration HYV seeds, and Green Revolution inputs. Madhya Pradesh has become the second-largest producer in recent years, overtaking Punjab.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: India's largest producer of tea is:
questions.explanation: Assam produces about 50 % of India's tea — chiefly in the Brahmaputra valley. West Bengal (Darjeeling, Dooars, Terai) is second; Tamil Nadu (Nilgiris) third. India is the world's second-largest tea producer after China. Assam tea is robust and malty; Darjeeling tea (WB) is floral and is often called the 'champagne of teas'.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The 'Green Revolution' in India during the 1960s-70s was driven primarily by the introduction of:
questions.explanation: The Green Revolution was led by M. S. Swaminathan in India and Norman Borlaug globally (Borlaug won the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize). It relied on HYV seeds — especially dwarf wheat (from CIMMYT, Mexico) and IR-8 rice (IRRI, Philippines) — combined with chemical fertilisers, pesticides and assured irrigation. Drip irrigation became widespread much later. It boosted yields but produced regional concentration (Punjab, Haryana, western UP) and environmental concerns like ground-water depletion.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: India's largest producer of sugarcane is:
questions.explanation: Uttar Pradesh is the top sugarcane producer by area and volume; Maharashtra is second and often leads in sugar production (because of higher sugar recovery per tonne of cane). India is the world's largest sugarcane producer and second-largest sugar producer after Brazil. Karnataka and Tamil Nadu are smaller but important.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The 'White Revolution' of India, which made the country the world's largest milk producer, is associated with:
questions.explanation: Verghese Kurien, 'Father of the White Revolution' / 'Milkman of India' — led Operation Flood (launched 1970) through the National Dairy Development Board. Built the Anand (Amul) cooperative model. India became the world's largest milk producer in 1998 and has held the position since. M. S. Swaminathan led the Green Revolution. Norman Borlaug worked on HYV wheat globally. Hargobind Khorana was a biochemist (Nobel 1968, genetic code).
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which of the following crops requires the most water for cultivation per hectare?
questions.explanation: Paddy rice is grown in flooded fields and typically needs 1,100-1,250 mm of water per crop cycle — far more than wheat (~400-500 mm), millets (300-400 mm) or pulses (which are often rain-fed). This is one reason rice cultivation in water-scarce Punjab and Haryana is being rethought in favour of less thirsty crops.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which state is the largest producer of sugarcane in India?
questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: Uttar Pradesh is the largest producer of sugarcane in India, accounting for about 40% of national production. It also has the highest number of sugar mills.

questions.stem: The 'Green Revolution' in India during the 1960s-70s primarily focused on:

options.option_text: High-yielding variety (HYV) seeds for wheat and rice

questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: The Green Revolution introduced high-yielding varieties (HYV) of wheat (Norman Borlaug's varieties adapted by M.S. Swaminathan) and rice, transforming India from food scarcity to surplus.

questions.stem: Rabi crops are sown in:
questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: Rabi crops (wheat, barley, mustard, gram) are winter crops sown in Oct–Nov and harvested in Mar–Apr. Kharif crops (rice, maize, cotton) are sown in June–July with monsoon.

questions.stem: The 'Golden Fibre' of India refers to:
questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: Jute is called the 'Golden Fibre' because of its golden and silky shine. West Bengal is the largest producer of jute in India.

questions.stem: Which state leads India in spice production?

options.option_text: Andhra Pradesh (closely followed by Kerala and Karnataka)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: Andhra Pradesh is India's largest spice producer by volume. Kerala is famous for high-value spices like pepper, cardamom (the 'Spice Garden of India').

questions.stem: India is the world's largest producer of which crop?

options.option_text: Milk / Pulses / Jute (India leads in several)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: India is the world's largest producer of milk (Operation Flood — White Revolution), pulses, jute, and banana. For rice and wheat, China leads.

questions.stem: The Zaid season refers to crops grown:

options.option_text: Between March and June (short summer season), e.g., cucumber, melon, watermelon

questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: Zaid crops are grown during the short summer season (March–June) between the Rabi and Kharif seasons. They include cucumbers, melons, gourds, and some vegetables.

questions.stem: Which state is called the 'Rice Bowl of India'?

options.option_text: Andhra Pradesh (also Chhattisgarh is sometimes called so)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: Andhra Pradesh (and sometimes Chhattisgarh) are referred to as the 'Rice Bowl of India' because of high rice cultivation. Punjab is the 'Wheat Bowl of India'.

questions.stem: Operation Flood, which launched India's 'White Revolution', was associated with:

options.option_text: Dairy development (led by Dr Verghese Kurien, AMUL model)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: Operation Flood (1970) was launched by the National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) under Dr. Verghese Kurien (the 'Milkman of India'), transforming India into the world's largest milk producer.

questions.stem: Which crop is known as the 'Brown Gold' of India?
questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: Coffee is known as 'Brown Gold'. India is a significant coffee producer; Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu are the major growing states.

questions.stem: Mixed farming refers to:

options.option_text: Growing multiple crops in a single field
Combining kharif and rabi on alternate years
Combining crop cultivation with animal husbandry on the same farm

questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: Mixed farming involves growing crops and raising livestock together on the same farm. The animals provide manure which enriches the soil for crops, creating a sustainable system.

questions.stem: Drip irrigation is most suitable for which type of crops?

options.option_text: Vegetables, fruits, and row crops where water can be delivered directly to roots

questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the root zone of individual plants, making it most efficient for horticulture, orchards, vegetables, and row crops. It is not used for flooded paddy.

questions.stem: The Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) is a scheme for:

options.option_text: Crop insurance for farmers against crop failure due to natural calamities

questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: PMFBY (2016) provides comprehensive risk insurance against crop failure due to non-preventable risks such as natural disasters, pests, and diseases at low premium rates for farmers.

questions.stem: Which state is the largest producer of groundnut in India?
questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: Gujarat is the leading state in groundnut (peanut) production in India, followed by Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu.

questions.stem: Jhum cultivation (slash-and-burn) is practiced in:

options.option_text: North-eastern India and some Adivasi communities

questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: Jhum (shifting cultivation) is practiced in the hilly and forested regions of northeast India (Nagaland, Mizoram, Manipur, Meghalaya) where forests are cleared by burning and used for a few seasons.

questions.stem: India's largest irrigation system by area is:

options.option_text: Canal irrigation (surface water canals — largest source of irrigation in India overall)

questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: Tube well / groundwater (underground) irrigation actually dominates in terms of area irrigated in modern India, especially in Punjab, Haryana, and UP. Canal irrigation is the oldest but groundwater now leads.

questions.stem: The soil best suited for cotton cultivation is:

options.option_text: Black (regur) soil — rich in clay, retains moisture

questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: Black cotton soil (regur/vertisol) is ideal for cotton due to its high moisture retention capacity, rich in minerals. The Deccan plateau states are major cotton producers.

questions.stem: Which Indian state leads in tea production?
questions.subject: Geography
questions.explanation: Assam is India's largest tea-producing state, contributing about 50% of India's tea output. Darjeeling is famous for quality premium tea, but Assam leads in volume.
